entry: American [[Game show|television game show]]. Two families compete to name the most popular answers to survey questions in order to win cash and prizes. Created by Mark Goodson, the show ran on ABC from 1976 to 1985, with Richard Dawson as host, and was revived in 1988 on [[CBS]]. Since 2010 it has been hosted by [[Steve Harvey]], whose tenure increased Nielsen ratings significantly and placed the program among the top three most-popular syndicated television shows in the United States.

American animated sitcom created by [[Seth MacFarlane]] for the [[Fox Broadcasting Company]]. It premiered on January 31, 1999, and centers on the Griffins, a dysfunctional family in the fictional city of Quahog, [[Rhode Island]]. Much of its humor takes the form of cutaway gags that often lampoon American culture. Fox revived the show in 2004 after its original run ended, following strong DVD sales and syndicated reruns. A 2009 Primetime Emmy Award nomination for Outstanding Comedy Series was the first for an animated series since [[The Flintstones]] in 1961. In April 2025 the show was renewed for four more seasons.

Planning of the number and timing of children, including the choice to have none. Aside from contraception, its aspects include [[Sex education|sex education]], pre-conception counseling and management, and [[Infertility|infertility]] management. As defined by the [[United Nations]] and the World Health Organization, family planning encompasses services leading up to conception, and [[Abortion|abortion]] is another form of it. The term is sometimes used as a synonym for access to contraception, although it often involves more. In 2006 the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommended that men and women formulate a reproductive life plan to avoid unintended pregnancies. Spacing births is associated with healthier pregnancies and lower risks of maternal morbidity, fetal prematurity and low birth weight. Family planning programs used by many developing countries between 1950 and 1995 are controversial because of coercion, primarily in [[China]], [[India]] and [[Peru]].

Person who exhibits strong interest or admiration for something or someone, such as a [[Celebrity|celebrity]], a sport, a genre, a politician or a television show. Also called an aficionado or enthusiast, a fan may promote the object of interest, join a fan club, attend conventions, write fan mail or create fan art, fan fiction or memes. Collectively, fans of an object form its [[Fandom|fanbase or fandom]]. Some excessively avid fans are called "stans." The word is a shortening of "fanatic," which entered English around 1550 from Modern Latin fanaticus, meaning "insanely but divinely inspired." The Great American Baseball Scrapbook attributes the term to Chris von der Ahe, owner of the Saint Louis Brown Stockings, who in 1882 called the patrons filling his stands "fans."

Subculture composed of [[Fan (person)|fans]] who feel camaraderie with others sharing a common interest. Fans often attend to minor details of their object of interest and devote much time and energy to it, frequently within a social network. A fandom can grow around any area of human interest, from a franchise or individual celebrity to a hobby, genre or fashion. The term has roots in enthusiasm for sports, and Merriam-Webster traces its usage to 1903. Many fandoms overlap, and conventions such as San Diego Comic-Con, WonderCon, Dragon Con and New York Comic Con draw large attendance. Feminist scholar Adrianne Wadewitz cited the devotees of [[Jane Austen]], the Janeites, as the earliest example of fandom, beginning around 1870. Media fandom split from [[Science fiction|science fiction]] fandom in the early 1970s, focusing on characters in franchises such as [[Star Trek]].

Dutch track and field athlete. Known as "the Flying Housewife," she won four gold medals at the 1948 [[Olympic Games|Summer Olympics]] in [[London]], where she competed as a 30-year-old mother of two and was the most successful athlete at the event. She began competing in athletics in 1935, set several world records during World War II and competed at the 1936 Olympics in [[Berlin]]. She won five European titles and 58 Dutch championships, and set or tied 12 world records, the last in the pentathlon in 1951 at age 33. She retired in 1955 and became captain of the Dutch female track and field team. In 1999 the International Association of Athletics Federations voted her "Female Athlete of the Century." Her Olympic victories are credited with helping to eliminate the belief that age and motherhood were barriers to success in women's sport.

1940 American animated anthology film produced by Walt Disney Productions. Its eight segments are set to classical music conducted by Leopold Stokowski and introduced by Deems Taylor. *Fantasia* was the first commercial film released in stereo, using the Fantasound system developed with RCA. Its initial roadshow release was a box-office failure, but repeated reissues from 1942 proved highly profitable. In 1990 it was selected for preservation in the U.S. National Film Registry by the [[Library of Congress]]. It is considered one of the greatest animated films ever made, and its 1999 sequel was *Fantasia 2000*.

Genre of speculative fiction involving supernatural or magical elements, often including completely imaginary realms and creatures. Its roots lie in fantasy literature and drama, and from the twentieth century it expanded into film, television, graphic novels, [[Manga|manga]], [[Animation|animation]] and [[Video game|video games]]. Anglophone literary critics often call it "fantastic literature." Unlike realistic fiction, which must attend to the history and natural laws of reality, fantasy uses worldbuilding to create settings that may be impossible in reality. It is distinguished from [[Science fiction|science fiction]] by plausibility: science fiction speculates within the scientifically plausible, while fantasy constructs the impossible. Fantasy elements appear in ancient texts such as the [[Epic of Gilgamesh]], in the comedies of [[Aristophanes]], and in the works of [[Ovid]] and [[Plato]], whose allegories influenced the genre.

Politics further to the left on the political spectrum than the standard political left. The far left encompasses a wide range of ideologies, including [[Anarchism|anarchism]], revolutionary socialism and [[Communism|communism]]. It frequently advocates anti-capitalism, anti-globalization, anti-imperialism and anti-fascism, with most aspiring to a classless and/or stateless society. Anarchists and democratic socialists strongly oppose authoritarianism, while Leninists advocate a temporary dictatorship of the proletariat, which mainstream Western scholarship generally characterizes as resulting in authoritarian governing structures. Some have used democratic methods, while others have resorted to political violence.

Politics further to the right on the political spectrum than the standard political right. Far-right ideologies are marked by ultraconservatism, ultranationalism, authoritarianism and radical anti-communism. Historically they include reactionary conservatism, [[Fascism|fascism]] and [[Nazism|Nazism]], while contemporary forms incorporate neo-fascism, [[Neo-Nazism|neo-Nazism]] and supremacism. Far-right politics emphasize postliberalist and exclusivist views, or opposition to liberal democracy, and a notion of societal purity based on a homogeneous community. In Western Europe they have often focused on anti-immigration and anti-globalism, while in the United States they emphasize nativism and opposition to an increasingly centralized federal government.

Hemisphere of the [[Moon]] that always faces away from [[Earth]]. Owing to [[Tidal locking|tidal locking]], it never fully comes into view from Earth, though about 18% is occasionally visible through libration. The remaining 82% was unobserved until the Soviet Luna 3 probe photographed it in 1959. Its rugged, heavily cratered terrain includes the South Pole–Aitken basin. China's Chang'e 4 made the first landing there in January 2019, and Chang'e 6 returned the first lunar samples from the far side on June 25, 2024. The nickname "dark side" means unseen rather than unlit; the far side is actually more reflective than the near side.

SI unit of electrical capacitance, equal to one coulomb per volt (C/V). It is named after [[Michael Faraday]], an English physicist. A capacitor has a capacitance of one farad when one [[Coulomb|coulomb]] of charge changes the potential between its plates by one [[Volt|volt]]. The farad is impractically large for most applications, so smaller units are used: 1 mF = 0.001 F, 1 μF = 10⁻⁶ F, 1 nF = 10⁻⁹ F and 1 pF = 10⁻¹² F. The term was coined in 1861 by Latimer Clark and Charles Bright and was officially adopted as the unit's name in 1881 at the International Congress of Electricians in Paris.

Enclosure of conductive material, usually mesh, that blocks some electromagnetic fields. Named after [[Michael Faraday]], who first built one in 1836, it works because an external field redistributes charges in the conductor so that the field cancels inside. Faraday cages protect sensitive electronics from radio-frequency interference and protect people and equipment from lightning and electrostatic discharges. They cannot block stable or slowly varying magnetic fields, such as the [[Earth's magnetic field]], so a compass still works inside one. Radio waves are heavily attenuated, though high-powered near-field transmissions such as HF RFID can penetrate.

Basic law of electromagnetism describing how a changing magnetic field induces an electric current in a circuit. This electromagnetic induction is the operating principle of [[Transformer|transformers]], inductors, many [[Electric motor|electric motors]], generators and solenoids. The term refers to two related statements: the Maxwell–Faraday equation, which holds that a time-varying magnetic field is accompanied by a circulating electric field, and the Faraday–Lenz law, which relates the electromotive force around a closed loop to the rate of change of magnetic flux through it. [[Michael Faraday]] demonstrated the effect in 1831.

Most populous city in [[North Dakota]], U.S. (pop., 2020: 125,990), and county seat of Cass County. Founded in 1871 on the Red River of the North floodplain, it forms the core of the Fargo–Moorhead metropolitan area with its twin city of Moorhead, Minnesota, which had a population of 248,591 in 2020. The city was originally named Centralia before being renamed for William Fargo, a founder of the Wells Fargo Express Company. On Labor Day in 1910, [[Theodore Roosevelt]] visited to lay the cornerstone of the college library. North Dakota State University is located in the city.

Area of land devoted primarily to agricultural production of food and other crops, including its farmhouse and agricultural buildings. The term has been extended to include wind farms and fish farms, and it covers ranches, orchards, plantations and hobby farms. About 570 million farms exist worldwide, most of them small and family-operated. Small farms of fewer than 2 [[Hectare|hectares]] operate on about 12% of the world's agricultural land, while family farms comprise about 75%. The transition from hunter-gatherer societies to settled agriculture is called the [[Neolithic Revolution]] and began about 12,000 years ago. By 4,000 BC people in central Europe were using [[Ox|oxen]] to pull plows and wagons. Later step-changes came with the British Agricultural Revolution of the 18th century and the [[Green Revolution]] of the 20th century. Modern farms in developed countries are highly mechanized.

Person engaged in agriculture, raising living organisms for food or raw materials. The term usually applies to those who raise field crops, orchards, vineyards, [[Poultry|poultry]] or other [[Livestock|livestock]]. In most developed economies a farmer is usually the landowner, while employees are known as farmhands. Over half a billion farmers are smallholders, mostly in developing countries, who economically support almost two billion people. Globally, women constitute more than 40% of agricultural employees. Ranchers in the United States and graziers in Australia and the U.K. raise grazing livestock, while a [[Dairy|dairy]] farmer is primarily engaged in milk production. Sharecroppers manage farmland for absentee owners and share the harvest. In the 1930s a U.S. farmer could feed only three other consumers; a modern farmer feeds well over a hundred people, though some authors consider that estimate flawed.

Archipelago in the North Atlantic Ocean and autonomous territory of [[Denmark]] (pop., 2026: 55,466). The islands lie between [[Iceland]], Norway and the Hebrides and Shetland of [[Scotland]], with a land area of 1,393 sq km (538 sq mi). The official language, Faroese, is partially mutually intelligible with Icelandic. The rugged terrain is dominated by [[Fjord|fjords]] and cliffs. The climate is mild year-round because of the [[Gulf Stream]], and the capital, Tórshavn, receives the fewest recorded hours of sunshine of any city in the world, 840 hours per year. Norse settlement dates to the early 9th century. The islands were ceded to Denmark in 1814 by the Treaty of Kiel. A 1946 referendum that narrowly favored independence was annulled by King Christian X, and home rule followed in 1948. Fishing accounts for around 90% of exports, and the islands are not part of the [[European Union]].

American actress. She rose to international fame as private investigator Jill Munroe in the first season of the television series *Charlie's Angels*. Her red swimsuit poster sold six million copies in its first year in print. She was a four-time Primetime Emmy Award nominee and six-time Golden Globe Award nominee, receiving Emmy nominations for playing a battered wife in *The Burning Bed* and a real-life murderer in *Small Sacrifices*. Her films include *The Apostle* (1997), with [[Robert Duvall]]. Fawcett was diagnosed with anal cancer in 2006, and the [[NBC]] documentary *Farrah's Story* (2009) chronicled her struggle with the disease.

Art of applying design, aesthetics, clothing construction and natural beauty to clothing and its accessories. It is influenced by diverse cultures and trends that have varied over time and place. A fashion designer creates garments such as dresses, suits, pants, skirts, shoes and handbags, and may specialize in clothing, accessories or jewelry. Designers may work in-house for a fashion house, freelance for houses, shops or manufacturers, or set up their own labels. Most designers work for apparel manufacturers on mass-market lines, while haute couture and bespoke tailoring are made for individual clients. Garment design weighs [[Color|color]], texture, lines, pattern, silhouette, shape, proportion, balance, emphasis, rhythm and harmony. Designers typically begin with patternmaking, starting from a base pattern, or sloper, that fits a model or standard size chart.

Algorithm for computing the [[Fourier transform|discrete Fourier transform]] (DFT), or its inverse, of a sequence. It reduces the complexity of computing the DFT from O(n²) to O(n log n), where n is the sequence length. Mathematically equivalent to the DFT, many FFT algorithms are also much more accurate in the presence of round-off error. The basic ideas were popularized in 1965 by James W. Cooley and John W. Tukey, who are generally credited with the modern generic algorithm. Some similar methods date to an unpublished 1805 work by [[Carl Friedrich Gauss|Gauss]] on asteroid orbits. In 1994 Gilbert Strang called the FFT "the most important numerical algorithm of our lifetime."

Mass-produced food designed for commercial resale, with a strong priority on speed of service. It is typically sold in restaurants or stores with frozen, preheated or precooked ingredients and served in packaging for takeaway. Fast food was created to accommodate busy commuters, travelers and wage workers, and the industry was worth an estimated $570 billion globally in 2018. Chains such as [[McDonald's]] and [[Burger King]] use pre-prepared ingredients but cook meat and french fries fresh before assembling orders. Outlets are traditionally distinguished by the drive-through. Many fast foods are high in saturated fat, sugar, salt and calories, and consumption has been linked to increased risk of [[Obesity|obesity]], [[Cardiovascular disease|cardiovascular disease]] and [[Colorectal cancer|colorectal cancer]]. Ready-cooked food for sale dates to urban life in [[Ancient Rome]], where street stands served food and drink.

Hardware device that mechanically joins or affixes two or more objects together. Fasteners generally create non-permanent joints that can be dismantled without damaging the joined components. Welding, soldering, gluing and sewing can create permanent joints instead. Common threaded fasteners include the screw, the [[Nut (hardware)|nut]] and bolt, possibly with washers. Metal fasteners are typically made of stainless, carbon or alloy steel, or of titanium or aluminum, and are often coated with zinc, chrome or hot-dip galvanizing to improve corrosion resistance. In 2005 the U.S. fastener industry was estimated to run 350 manufacturing plants and employ 40,000 workers. More than 200 billion fasteners are used per year in the United States, 26 billion of them by the automotive industry. Selection depends on accessibility, environment, installation process, materials, reusability and weight restrictions.

Propagation of matter or information faster than the speed of light in vacuum. [[Special relativity|Special relativity]] holds that only particles with zero rest mass, such as photons, can travel at the [[Speed of light|speed of light]], and that nothing can travel faster. Hypothetical particles called [[Tachyon|tachyons]] would violate [[Causality (physics)|causality]] and imply time travel, and the scientific consensus is that they do not exist. Speculative proposals include the Alcubierre drive, Krasnikov tubes, traversable [[Wormhole|wormholes]] and quantum tunneling. Such proposals are widely believed to be impossible, as they still violate current understandings of causality and require exotic matter.

Willing abstinence from, or reduced consumption of, food or drink. Physiologically, fasting may refer to the metabolic status of a person who has not eaten overnight, or to the state reached after digestion of a meal, which typically begins 3–5 hours after eating. Fasting is almost always practiced before [[Surgery|surgery]] or procedures requiring general anesthesia, to reduce the risk of aspiration. Intermittent fasting is used for weight loss or other health benefits. Alternate-day fasting has been shown to improve cardiovascular and metabolic biomarkers similarly to calorie restriction in overweight or obese people. Prolonged fasting, typically 5–20 days, shifts the body toward [[Ketone|ketosis]], and weight loss averages 0.9 kg per day in the first week. The longest documented fast was that of Scottish man Angus Barbieri, who fasted for 382 days from June 14, 1965, to June 30, 1966. Fasting may also be part of a religious ritual or a hunger strike.
